subject: Banking
title: Cybersecurity and Digital Trust
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Cybersecurity and Digital Trust.

hook.text: The 2019 Capital One breach exposed 100 million customer records.

buildup.text: Banks are the number one target for cyberattacks. Financial data is the most valuable data.

discovery.text: Banks spend over $10 billion annually on cybersecurity.

twist.text: The weakest link is usually human. Phishing emails trick employees into revealing credentials.

climax.text: Digital banking requires digital trust. One breach can destroy decades of reputation.

punchline.text: 100 million records from one firewall error. Trust is fragile and expensive.

quiz.question: What caused the Capital One data breach?

details.summary: As banking moves entirely digital, cybersecurity becomes the foundation of customer trust. Banks spend billions defending against constantly evolving threats including ransomware, social engineering, and state-sponsored attacks on financial infrastructure.
details.whyItMatters: A single major cybersecurity breach can destroy decades of customer trust in minutes. In digital banking, security is not just an IT issue but the core product feature that determines whether customers trust the institution with their money.
takeaways: Banks are the most targeted industry for cyberattacks globally
Financial institutions spend over 10 percent of IT budgets on security
Social engineering attacks on employees remain the weakest link

faq.question: What is the biggest cybersecurity threat to banks?
faq.answer: Social engineering, where attackers manipulate employees into granting access, remains the most effective attack vector. Technical defenses are strong, but human error and deception bypass technological safeguards regularly.

faq.question: How much do banks spend on cybersecurity?
faq.answer: Major banks spend over a billion dollars annually on cybersecurity. JPMorgan alone spends roughly 15 billion per year on technology, with a significant portion dedicated to security. The spending grows as threats become more sophisticated.
